title: Phones to be banned from pupils' bags or pockets under new rules
description: Pupils will not be allowed to have their phones on them at all during the school day under stricter government guidance in England.Statutory guidance
body: Pupils will not be allowed to have their phones on them at all during the school day under stricter government guidance in England.Statutory guidance came into force in June, making schools and trusts legally responsible for being phone-free throughout the day.Ministers now say changes to that guidance will go beyond the current "no see, no hear" policies in place in some schools - where phones can remain in pupils' bags if they are not seen or heard - when it comes into force from September 2027.But head teachers' unions said schools would struggle to implement stricter new policies without additional funding from government.Education Secretary Lucy Powell said the government's "clear message" to parents and pupils was that "school is for learning and friendship, not scrolling".Access to phones "risks pulling children away from their learning and from each other", the government said.Schools will be able to decide how to follow the guidance. Some schools have invested in sealed pouches or secure lockers. Others collect phones at the start of the day, or have prohibited them from sites altogether.Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the NAHT school leaders union, said phones could raise "safety issues" and be an "unhelpful distraction" during the school day. But he said the more robust measures recommended under the new guidance would "come at a cost".Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said the latest guidance "does at least provide some clarity", but added that school leaders "cannot simply make mobile phones disappear"."If all schools are going to be expected to have lockable pouches or other secure storage facilities for every pupil, the cost involved will be very significant indeed," he said."This is not feasible unless the government puts in the funding required to meet these costs."Dame Rachel de Souza, Children's Commissioner for England, said she welcomed strong action to stop phones distracting pupils and disrupting the school day.Charlotte Ashton, co-founder of campaign group of Generation Focus, similarly welcomed the changes, saying "no see, no hear" policies were not working and pupils were still "TikToking in the toilets"."Ultimately, we need to get to a point where it's not normal for every single child to have a personal internet-enabled device in their pockets with them 24/7," she said.Shadow Education Secretary Laura Trott said she was "delighted that Labour have finally listened to us and agreed to properly ban smartphones in schools".She said it was also the "right thing to do" to have a review of safety standards around the technology used in schools, which the government has also announced on the back of calls for improved guidance.But she criticised what she called a lack of "joined up thinking" over what new tech was being allowed in classrooms.Because education is devolved, the approach to phones in schools varies across the UK.In Scotland, external, the government has said it will introduce a new law to restrict the personal use of phones in schools, and launched a consultation on the issue over the summer.In Wales, external, the Senedd recently voted against a motion to introduce a national statutory ban on phones in classrooms. Schools are still encouraged to restrict the use of phones during the school day, but heads have flexibility over how to implement their own rules.And in Northern Ireland, Education Minister Paul Givan launched a 12-week consultation in August on whether to ban mobile phones from schools by law, calling for "a stronger and more consistent approach across our education system".Rules around phones in schools are separate from the UK's upcoming ban on social media for under-16s, due to be introduced in March.Children will be barred from accessing platforms like Instagram, Snapchat and TikTok. Vinted and eBay could also be included in the list of platforms set to be banned, the culture secretary has said.Additional reporting by Beth Rose and Nathan Standley

schema.headline: Phones to be banned from pupils' bags or pockets under new rules

title: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
description: Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the boss of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.The US President said he spoke with ch
body: Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the boss of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.The US President said he spoke with chief executive Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign."I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.China has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".Nvidia, who has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.But later on Monday, Trump said the FBI was now looking into the issue, but did not elaborate on the probe or when it was launched. The BBC has contacted the FBI. US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report.The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia, the company at the centre at the development of AI worldwide through its microchips.The American firm run, co-founded by Huang, is also a major focus in the AI rivalry between the US and China, with officials treating the company's exports to Beijing as a matter of national security.Trump, at a Monday afternoon news conference, said he thought Huang was an "honorable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape"."I did speak to him today just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing, and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy," the president said.Trump added he was "sure" China president Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met.Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyondNvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spyWhat we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spyHuang has admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He said on Monday he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation the company had launched. Huang has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.In the letter, the chairmen of the committees said they were seeking a briefing "on Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang".It's unclear whether Huang will appear. The BBC has contacted Nvidia and the committees.

schema.headline: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy

title: Russell Brand's ex Jemima Goldsmith accuses him of violence and abuse against her
description: Warning - this report contains graphic content.Jemima Goldsmith, the ex-girlfriend of Russell Brand, has accused him of "violence, coercive control an
body: Warning - this report contains graphic content.Jemima Goldsmith, the ex-girlfriend of Russell Brand, has accused him of "violence, coercive control and abuse" while the two were together.Goldsmith, who dated the disgraced entertainer for roughly a year around 2014, alleged that she "had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident" but chose not to press charges.In a lengthy statement on social media, the 52-year-old said she was "in awe of the courageous women who came forward at Brand's trial" and was "glad and relieved" he had "finally faced justice".Brand, 51, was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison earlier on Monday after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.He was found guilty of raping a woman at his home in 2009, as well as three counts of sexual assault against three other women. The judge at the sentencing hearing told Brand that he harboured a "casual arrogant disregard to any woman's right to say no to you", while his fame meant he believed "you could act when you liked and how you liked".TV producer Goldsmith is also the former wife of ex-Pakistani prime minister and cricketer Imran Khan, the daughter of late billionaire entrepreneur Sir James Goldsmith and sister of ex-Conservative government minister Zac Goldsmith.The mother-of-two said she had chosen not to pursue legal recourse against Brand over the alleged violent incident in 2014 as she was "worried about the impact of the press attention on my then teenage children".She wrote on X on Monday evening: "Whilst my pain in relation to this pales in comparison to what the women have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact."Goldsmith said she had not seen nor spoken to Brand since 2014, but claimed to have assisted the journalists who exposed the allegations against him and had been willing to testify to his "abusiveness" were they sued.In her statement, she also addressed reports of an injunction taken out by her and Brand in October 2015 that banned a woman, Szilvia Berki, from harassing them including by making allegations of assault by Brand at Goldsmith's home the prior year.Goldsmith said on Monday that Berki had visited her house for roughly 30 minutes on 7 June 2014 to give Brand a massage, which she said did not end up taking place once she arrived.Goldsmith said that Berki later told police that Brand had pushed her in the back while she had been leaving and that she had been attacked by Goldsmith's dog. Brand's ex-girlfriend said she "did not see anything untoward" during the encounter.She added that, after providing a statement and CCTV footage, police concluded that there was no case to answer.Goldsmith accused Berki of then sending a series of "vicious antisemitic and threatening" messages and posting "wild and untrue allegations" about her on social media.She said she then agreed to a suggestion from Brand's lawyer to seek an injunction to prevent harassment. She claimed on Monday that recent media reporting of the injunction had opened her up "to vile hatred and abuse online".Sunday Times chief news correspondent Rosamund Urwin, who was involved in a media investigation into Brand in 2023, has told the BBC that Goldsmith helped her "a lot"."I have seen the abuse she's been getting online and I did try to tell people that part of the story was much more complicated than they realise," Urwin said. "I wish people would remember women that come forward are brave people and that is what she has done tonight – she has spoken out with immense bravery about how Russell Brand treated her," she added.Brand's sentencing hearing heard victim impact statements from the women he had been accused of assaulting.One of them said she was "upset and traumatised" for years after the incident, adding: "I didn't have any respect for myself. I was thinking I was damaged goods - scared of giving off signals that could be taken the wrong way."The woman he was found guilty of raping said the trauma was something she had to "carry every day".A van believed to be carrying Brand was seen arriving at HMP Wandsworth in London on Monday after the sentencing hearing.

schema.headline: Russell Brand's ex Jemima Goldsmith accuses him of violence and abuse against her

title: How a civil servant got away with juggling five jobs for so long
description: Little did she know UKHSA was not Chowdhury's only employer.That month, he was also being paid to work full-time for the Department for the Environmen
body: Little did she know UKHSA was not Chowdhury's only employer.That month, he was also being paid to work full-time for the Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the Department for Business and Trade, the Food Standards Agency and the Home Office. He was contracted to work 183 hours a week – more than the number of hours in seven days. He fraudulently earned more than £284,000 of taxpayers' money.In total, he had eight overlapping full-time public-sector jobs between 2020 and 2023. During that time, this relatively junior civil servant was paid £350,000.Soon after her call with Chowdhury, Adams discovered that he had logged into the call using a Defra email address. When she challenged him about it, he blamed it on a technical error. She told the jury at his trial at Southwark Crown Court: "I believed he was lying." She escalated her concerns up the chain.But his fraudulent behaviour remained undetected. Chowdhury was able to keep working multiple government jobs until September 2023 when he left the Civil Service.He was finally caught in 2024 by the government's National Fraud Initiative, which conducts searches of Civil Service databases, such as payroll, every two years to look for anomalies.On Monday he was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and told by the judge that he would be facing a "very substantial custodial sentence".Chowdhury, 56, arrived each day at court alone. He is married, yet there never seemed to be any friends or family there to support him.He would often make his way down the corridors of the court building carrying two plastic carrier bags, with a bobble hat perched on his head.He sometimes looked bewildered in the witness box. Chowdhury, who had a diagnosis of PTSD in 2015, said that he had taken on so many roles because he feared losing his livelihood after experiencing insecure employment. He said he'd been forced out of a job at the Department for Education in 2013.He said he hadn't been thinking clearly when applying for jobs ''because of my stress, distress and trauma and due to my panic at the time".But the prosecution argued his behaviour was "deliberate" and "intentional dishonesty" and that he had exploited the system. However, the case raises important questions for the Civil Service. How was he able to get away with it for so long?Part of the explanation is that the Civil Service's human resources system is not centralised. Chowdhury did not declare on government application forms that he was already a civil servant, so the system did not spot the duplication.Hannah Keenan, who works at the Institute for Government, says the system clearly failed. "Government departments are taking hiring decisions independently of each other and without systems that join up," she said. "That the model and the culture surrounding it aren't working shouldn't be a surprise though - we've known for a long time about poor performers flying under the radar by shuffling between jobs."There are more than 550,000 people employed across the Civil Service, many in offices in Whitehall, in central London. They are responsible for carrying out government policy and the daily administration of the country.Another reason why Chowdhury's fraud went undetected is that he was working entirely from the east London house he shared with his mother. In 2023, she had dementia and terminal cancer, and he told his employers that he needed to be at home to look after her.But rather than reducing his workload to concentrate on her care, he took on more jobs. He covered up his impossible daily schedule by getting sick notes from his GP.In April 2023, he was off with what he called "mixed anxiety and depressive disorder" from Defra, the UKHSA, the Department for Business and Trade and the Food Standards Agency.While the sick notes were shown to the jury, they were not given evidence about what caused the depressive disorder or of a psychiatric assessment having been done during this period.His sickness did not prevent him from starting yet another job – this time at the Home Office. He did not mention to them he was ill, nor did he tell them he was working elsewhere.Unsurprisingly, a succession of his line managers told the jury he had not been very good at his jobs.Especially damning was the evidence given by Dan McCartney, who managed Chowdhury at Defra. He said he had to "effectively tell him what to do the whole time" and that Chowdhury kept his camera off during video calls for four months, claiming technical problems.But because Chowdhury was not subject to any formal performance measures at Defra, he was given a permanent job. He remained there for two years.In September 2023, Chowdhury was found to have more than £40,000 in his bank accounts as well as significant investments, including £45,000 in premium bonds.A recent survey of 1,700 civil servants by the independent think tank Re:State found 76% of respondents thought it did not do a good job of tackling poor performers.An ex-senior civil servant told the BBC that much of the Civil Service is culturally averse to performance management."Whitehall's known for ages it has to be less risk averse. Shrinking the Civil Service and the adoption of artificial intelligence technology make that more vital," they said. "But don't underestimate the fear factor: fear of drawn-out grievances and fear of being accused of wasting taxpayers' money if the Civil Service was to do what big private sector firms do, which is cut to get rid of poor performers by offering some money and a settlement agreement."A Defra spokesperson said: "Kashim Chowdhury abused the trust placed in him as a public servant and defrauded taxpayers out of almost £285,000. He will now rightly face the consequences for his actions."This conviction is the result of a thorough and painstaking investigation led by the Defra Counter Fraud and Investigations team. It sends a clear message that fraud against the public purse will not be tolerated and those responsible will be held to account."The spokesperson said Defra would use "all available avenues to recover the proceeds of Chowdhury's offending on behalf of taxpayers". Chowdhury's case also illustrates a wider issue.He was engaged in what is being called "polygamous working", where people hold down several jobs secretly. Websites have even been set up offering people advice on how to keep their employers in the dark.Its rise has been blamed on larger numbers of people working from home.The government's National Fraud Initiative has identified 23 cases of "polygamous working" across London in its most recent report. It uncovered £500,000 of overpaid salaries over a period of a few months. Alongside the fraud case, Chowdhury is involved in a legal dispute with his three siblings, who accuse him of ''bullying'' their mother into signing over half of her £2.1m home to him in the final days of her life. He denies it.At times during his criminal trial, Chowdhury appeared confused by what he was hearing and blamed trauma for the web of lies he had spun. The jury took seven hours to reach their verdict and decided he was motivated by personal gain - stealing tens of thousands of pounds from the taxpayer.Chowdhury now faces a significant custodial sentence.

schema.headline: How a civil servant got away with juggling five jobs for so long

title: Russell Brand sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for rape and sexual assault
description: Figure caption, Watch: Moment judge sentences Russell Brand in courtBySima KotechaSenior UK correspondentReporting fromSouthwark Crown Court and Steve
body: Figure caption, Watch: Moment judge sentences Russell Brand in courtBySima KotechaSenior UK correspondentReporting fromSouthwark Crown Court and Steven McIntoshWarning - this report contains graphic content.Russell Brand has been sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison, after being convicted of rape and sexual assault. In his sentencing remarks, judge Joel Bennathan described Brand as a "sexual predator" and criticised his "staggering arrogance".The 51-year-old was sentenced to nine years for rape, with an additional 18 months, nine months and eight months for three counts of sexual assault. The disgraced entertainer was found guilty of the charges involving four women between 2004 and 2009. Brand did not react in the dock as he was sentenced. Before being taken down to the cells, he mouthed "I love you" to his wife Laura Brand, who was in the court.The guidelines state offenders jailed for four years or more for some serious violent or sexual offences will be released at the two thirds point. In Brand's case that would be seven years.Once released, he is likely to spend the rest of his sentence on licence and will have to abide by specific rules such as wearing a tag. His sentence will not be included in the early release scheme. Sex offenders, along with murderers, are exempt from the scheme.The judge also paid tribute to the bravery of the women who gave evidence during the trial.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Laura Brand was pictured as she left court following her husband's sentencingIn total, Brand was sentenced to:Nine years' imprisonment for anally raping a 21-year-old in 2009 at his home in LondonNine months for sexually assaulting a woman whose breasts he grabbed at a bar in London in 2004 during a birthday partyEighteen months for sexually assaulting a woman at the Choice FM studios in London in 2004 or 2005, when he grabbed her face and kissed her before touching her breasts and bottomEight months for sexual assault while working on a Channel 4 project in 2009, when he laid his head into the groin area of a woman working with him without her consentImage source, Elizabeth Cook/Press AssociationIn further remarks, the judge said Brand's status protected him until 2023, when journalists from the Sunday Times, the Times and Channel 4's Dispatches outlined a series of misconduct allegations, leading to women making complaints to police. He said Brand harboured a "casual arrogant disregard to any woman's right to say no to you", while his fame meant he believed "you could act when you liked and how you liked".The judge said the evidence in the case also showed that Brand's entourage during the peak of his celebrity had "indulged your dreadful behaviour".Before Brand's sentencing, the court heard victim impact statements from the women he had been accused of assaulting.One of the women, who spoke from behind a screen, said she had been in "shock and turmoil for years"."I was extremely upset and traumatised," she said. "I didn't have any respect for myself. I was thinking I was damaged goods - scared of giving off signals that could be taken the wrong way."She added: "I just want to say - a leopard may change its spots but it's still a leopard."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Russell Brand pictured outside court earlier this monthBrand left victim 'anxious and humiliated'"Russell Brand has managed to move on," a woman, who was sexually assaulted by Brand in 2005, said in a statement read out in court. "This has had a lasting impact on my life. I recognise this now."However, over the years, hearing his voice on television or seeing his image has made me jump. I had a strong adverse reaction hearing his voice."She added: "Russell Brand is a sexual predator who has no remorse... I just hope he is not allowed to hurt any more women."A statement from the woman Brand was found to have raped was also shared in court."I felt anxious, humiliated and overwhelmed," she said. "I struggled to sleep and eat, I struggled to cope with my emotions, I had to take time away from my work," she said. She continued: "I had to live with my parents, I sought help and support... I am living with trauma, something I carry every day."My confidence and self esteem have been badly affected. I no longer trust my instincts."The woman said one of the worst parts of what happened was her fear that she might have contracted HIV. She also said she was in considerable pain after the assault.A woman, who was sexually assaulted while working on a Channel 4 project with Brand in 2009, said in a statement that she was "really upset" afterwards. "I felt I lost my trust in people, I felt my working environment wasn't safe," she said. "I felt powerless in that moment and it had a knock-on effect on my confidence."Image source, Elizabeth Cook/Press AssociationImage caption, In his sentencing remarks, Mr Justice Bennathan described Brand as a "sexual predator"The verdicts were delivered on Thursday following a four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court in London.Brand was found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.He will automatically have to sign the Sex Offences' Register as part of his sentence because of the crimes he committed.Laura Brand was seated just a few feet away from the former comedian in the glass-walled dock as he was being sentenced.Earlier, as he arrived in the dock on Monday morning, Brand mouthed to his wife: "It'll be okay, I don't know how, but it will", and he was seen praying and making a cross sign with his hand as the victim statements were read out.Brand's barrister Ian Winter KC put forward six character references, including one from Georgina Baillie, the granddaughter of the late actor Andrew Sachs.Baillie was thrust into the spotlight in 2008 when Brand and Jonathan Ross left offensive messages about her on her grandfather's answering machine during a Radio 2 broadcast.Winter also told the court that the former entertainer's wife Laura Brand, who gave evidence in her husband's defence during the trial, was experiencing "total devastation" at the verdicts. He said Mr and Mrs Brand were "currently wrestling with how to exactly explain to a child who's just turned 10 what has happened here"."It brings home the consequences of this conduct to totally innocent people who have been caught up in it," he said.Sentencing Brand, the judge said: "I am very conscious that your imprisonment will deprive your children of the presence of their father. "That sad loss to them, however, is caused by your serious offending."Russell Brand on TrialYou can follow analysis and further insights on the BBC podcast Russell Brand on Trial - available on BBC Sounds, YouTube, iPlayer, or wherever you get your BBC podcasts

schema.headline: Russell Brand sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for rape and sexual assault

title: Michael Carrick: Manchester United expected to sack head coach
description: Manchester United look increasingly likely to sack head coach Michael Carrick.The club opted to stick with Carrick after the side's 3-0 home defeat by
body: Manchester United look increasingly likely to sack head coach Michael Carrick.The club opted to stick with Carrick after the side's 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October, with the intention of reassessing the situation during this month's international break. Multiple sources have told BBC Sport that the board remain committed to that process, and that no final decision on Carrick's future has been made.However, there is a growing expectation that chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox will recommend to minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazer family for Carrick to be sacked. The 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday means United, who are 18th in the table, have made their worst start to a domestic campaign in 40 years. BBC Sport reported in October that the club had sounded out former Newcastle boss Eddie Howe and ex-Germany coach Julian Nagelsmann over replacing Carrick.Former Chelsea coach Antonio Conte is known to be keen on the role, while multiple sources have told BBC Sport that former Spurs boss Mauricio Pochettino is open to a move to Old Trafford. Pochettino signed an extension to his contract as USA coach in August. However, the deal is thought to contain clauses that would allow him to leave for specific high-profile jobs. The US have a two-legged Concacaf Nations League play-off with Haiti on 14 and 18 November.The Villa draw was Carrick's third match in charge since the club opted to give the 45-year-old more time at Old Trafford.Results during that time - a win, a draw and a defeat - were mixed, and displayed the best and worst of Carrick's reign with United shipping goals but displaying good character to come back from two goals down on three occasions. United's board toyed with sacking Carrick after the loss to Bournemouth, but decided the Englishman - and his players - had earned the opportunity to show that they could turn the club's fortunes around.It was also felt that the two-week international break in November represented a better chance for the club to properly assess the club's start to the campaign.Unfortunately for Carrick, it makes for poor reading.With one victory in 10 Premier League matches, United have made their worst start to a top-flight campaign since the 1986/87 season.They sit 18th in the table, one point above bottom-placed Crystal Palace.Only the Eagles and Ipswich have conceded more than the 19 goals United have shipped in the Premier League this season.It is hard to believe given the club's current predicament just how quickly Carrick's tenure has soured.Looking back, the 48 hours before United's season-opening match at Hull were pivotal.With Benjamin Sesko still trying to ease his way back from the shin issue that ended his previous campaign early, Amad Diallo suffered an ankle injury that would rule him out for seven weeks. It meant Carrick was deprived of his first-choice striking alternative, with Bryan Mbeumo having to play on the right of the attack.Carrick instead turned to Matheus Cunha, whose preference for dropping deep took him into the spaces captain Bruno Fernandes likes to occupy.It neutralised United's attack on a day they seemed ill-prepared to meet the physical challenge of an opponent motivated by their long-awaited Premier League return.In his role as interviewer for Nordic broadcaster Viaplay, former Norway and Middlesbrough striker Jan Aage Fjortoft later claimed United had lacked passion - something Carrick dismissed as "ridiculous"."It's one game," Carrick told the media afterwards.The following week, United were losing to Ipswich - another newly promoted side. Only a slip from Marcelino Nunez inside his own half allowed Cunha to tee up Fernandes for an undeserved equaliser. The Portugal playmaker, who had just been crowned PFA Player of the Year for 2025-26, went on to complete a hat-trick in a 5-2 win.He has scored just once - a penalty against Villa on Sunday - in the league since.After the Ipswich win came a trip to Everton. Twice United led, the second occasion when Sesko struck two minutes from full-time after coming on as a substitute. Deep into stoppage time, Ainsley Maitland-Niles drove home from long range to deny the visitors.Asked how confident he was in his side's ability to react to a disappointing start to the season, Carrick snapped back: "It's not been that bad."What happened next, however, was.Time and again, United's fitness was called into question. They struggled badly against a Manchester City side reduced to 10 men in the first half before their rivals benefited from an Erling Haaland goal that referees' chief Howard Webb later admitted should not have stood.Carrick's complaints were justified - but they masked a poor performance from his team.After taking a 2-0 lead inside 10 minutes against Brighton in the EFL Cup, United were outplayed and beaten, thanks to two goals in four second-half minutes.The fine margins United benefited from during Carrick's interim spell were now going against them, and his coaching staff - lauded months earlier - could not find an answer.Carrick called Cunha's injury-time equaliser against a Fulham side who started the game bottom of the table a positive to build on. But immediately after the international break, United were held to another draw - conceding in injury time to an out-of-form and 10-man Tottenham.The whirlwind was starting to pick up strength.Lisandro Martinez, who scored an own goal against Fulham, was at fault for Spurs' leveller, which made his post-match outburst after the 2-0 Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid more amazing.The Argentina defender criticised United's summer recruitment and placed the blame at the door of "the technical director" - Wilcox.By the time of Martinez's outburst, Sesko and left-back Luke Shaw were injured. Marcus Rashford has not played since. The rotation at left-back that eventually led to Carrick starting five different players in that role was in full swing.After conceding in the opening minute against Atletico, Como scored inside the first two in a 4-1 Champions League defeat for United. Fernandes came out afterwards and criticised Carrick's tactics.He was dropped for the Bournemouth game, but returned as captain at Chelsea. United were beaten in both matches.With just three wins in 15 matches in all competitions this season and United stuck in 18th in the Premier League, Carrick is set to pay the price.

schema.headline: Michael Carrick: Manchester United expected to sack head coach

title: Booker Prize 2026: M John Harrison's 'baffling but brilliant' novel The End of Everything wins
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, M John Harrison was billed by Booker bosses as "a genuinely original thinker"ByIan YoungsCulture reporterAuth
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, M John Harrison was billed by Booker bosses as "a genuinely original thinker"ByIan YoungsCulture reporterAuthor M John Harrison has become the oldest ever winner of the Booker Prize, picking up the prestigious literary award for his post-apocalyptic novel The End of Everything.Harrison, 81, who has built a cult following over his 60-year career, was named the winner of the £50,000 prize at a ceremony in London on Monday.The End of Everything is set in the years after a mysterious catastrophe that caused British society as we know it to collapse. It has divided opinion among readers, and was described as "bleak but brilliant" and "dreamlike and baffling" by one critic.Dame Mary Beard, who chaired the Booker judges, said: "It's a challenging read, but some of the best fiction is challenging."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Harrison (far left) with his fellow nominees (left-right) Elizabeth Strout, Luke Kennard, Rebecca Perry, Marlon James and Douglas StuartDame Mary added: "It's a book that turns you upside down, raises a wry smile – and surprisingly, given the subject matter, leaves you with a twinge of optimism."Harrison began writing in the 1960s and has published 13 novels, five short story collections and an "anti-memoir". He has now surpassed Margaret Atwood as the oldest ever Booker winner.While he dislikes labels like science fiction and fantasy, he has been called "the titan of literary science fiction", and Booker Prize chief executive Gaby Wood said he is "the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world"."He is a genuinely original thinker, a genre-defying writer who takes ideas seriously," Wood said."Though very unsettling, The End of Everything is not in fact a strange book. It's a realist book about a strange world, populated by desperate, unmoored characters."Listen back to a special edition of BBC Radio 4 Front Row from the Booker Prize ceremony'Tender, terrifying and timely'The story follows a man and his aunt who must muddle through on the south-east English coast in the aftermath of an unexplained disaster and the arrival of mysterious alien beings.The author has said he deliberately omitted as much explanation about the background to the events as possible, in order to make readers feel the same disorientation as the characters.He has said: "The End of Everything is about trying to live as if nothing has gone wrong. It's a disaster story in which the disaster is the failure to comprehend."He added: "I've passed on to the reader some of the puzzlement and confusion of the characters in the book as they face a future with the alien."That approach has led to a mixed reaction. The Guardian praised the book but said, external "it won't be for everyone", while the New York Times said, external: "The more we learn about the conditions of this novel's broken world, the harder it is to grasp."The Literary Review described it as, external "a work of uncanny beauty, tender and terrifying in equal parts", while the Telegraph said, external "you feel you're not so much reading as dreaming".Another Telegraph critic wrote, external that it was "ultimately, in both skill and humour, a cut above" the other shortlisted books."And in an age when AI overlords keep threatening to kill us, and the Government has told us to stockpile tinned food and bottled water, it is, for once, a novel that you can genuinely call 'timely'."The Booker Prize is an annual award for the best novel written in the English language and published in the year up to 30 September. It was launched in 1969.This year's other shortlisted books were:The Disappearers by Marlon JamesBlack Bag by Luke KennardMay We Feed the King by Rebecca PerryThe Things We Never Say by Elizabeth StroutJohn of John by Douglas StuartWhen the shortlist was announced in September, Dame Mary said agreeing on the final six had been, "to put it mildly, hard work".Another judge, US novelist Patricia Lockwood, said she had been "tossing books across the room" during judging sessions, while poet Raymond Antrobus described the selection as "a tussle".The other judges were Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, and journalist, editor and critic Rebecca Liu.Speaking about the final judging session, Dame Mary told reporters on Monday:  "There was a lot of discussion, disagreement and debate. But nobody stomped off."In a statement, she said the panel "spent a whole day debating the six remarkable novels on this year's shortlist" before reaching a unanimous decision to name Harrison the winner.

schema.headline: Booker Prize 2026: M John Harrison's 'baffling but brilliant' novel The End of Everything wins

title: Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case
description: Prosecutors in the closely watched case alleged that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and
body: Prosecutors in the closely watched case alleged that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months - in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home.After weeks of emotional testimony, the jury took a week to deliberate, repeatedly telling the judge that they could not reach a verdict. The deadlock stemmed from a lone juror who voted to convict Clancy of first-degree murder, while the 11 other jurors intended to acquit Clancy by reason of insanity.In Massachusetts, as well as in all US criminal murder trials, juries must reach a unanimous decision to convict or acquit a defendant. Because the jurors failed to unanimously agree on whether the prosecution had proved Clancy was guilty "beyond a reasonable doubt" as required by US law, the judge declared a mistrial on 4 September, which means that she was neither found guilty nor not guilty.Clancy is currently being housed in a state-run psychiatric hospital and medical facility in Massachusetts. Ana Faguy contributed reporting.

schema.headline: Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case

title: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking
description: France has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges a
body: France has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers across the country last month.Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression", adding those who were responsible would be hit with sanctions.Iran has yet to respond officially, but some Iranian media outlets have dismissed the allegations as baseless.The French hacking, which led to the destruction of tons of frozen and chilled food in France was followed by a similar attack against supermarkets across several other European countries. It is not known if the instances are linked.Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people".He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act". France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.The Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with the IRGC as well as his two deputies.Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime.In recent weeks, a number of commentators and politicians in Iran have argued that the country should extend any retaliation beyond the Middle East if the US and Israel resume the war they started earlier this year. If the IRGC carried out the cyber-attacks, it remains unclear whether they were part of Iran's deterrence strategy.On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.More than 100 of Coopérative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe. Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in countries including Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.Separately in August a small number of US military bases had fridges mysteriously malfunction, spoiling food. This incident is also being investigated as deliberate cyber-attacks, Reuters news agency has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects.In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them.The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber-attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.Additional reporting by Farshad Bayan, BBC Persian.

schema.headline: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking

title: Krakow shooting suspect has died in hospital, police say
description: A gunman suspected of killing six people in central Krakow, as well as his parents and sister at their home, died in hospital early on Monday, Polish
body: A gunman suspected of killing six people in central Krakow, as well as his parents and sister at their home, died in hospital early on Monday, Polish police have said.The 24-year-old, who has been named as Michal Oksinski by local media, was injured after opening fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland, on Saturday, police said.Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the suspect, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said.Authorities initially reported that the gunman had apparently been inspired by "far-right ideologies", but have since said they are investigating any possible motivation.After the shooting, which began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's busy Main Market Square, police identified the attacker as a 24-year-old Polish man. In the hours after the shooting, a minister said that early investigations indicate he was inspired by "far-right ideologies". The minister also described him as an "ultra-nationalist" without giving further details.However, during a press briefing on Monday morning, Przemysław Nowak, a spokesperson for Poland's National Prosecutor's Office, said investigations into his motive remain ongoing.Six people - four women and two men - are confirmed to have been killed in the  attack.Four victims are Polish, while a British national and an Austrian woman were also killed.Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three bodies - two women and one man - were found at the gunman's house when it was searched after the attack.On Sunday, Polish police confirmed those three victims had been identified as the alleged gunman's 53-year-old father, 52-year-old mother and 21-year-old sister.Polish media has reported the suspect had a firearms permit and may have obtained the weapons from his family home.Four firearms were found in the gunman's car, including two AR-15 rifles and two handguns, along with several hundred rounds of ammunition, Nowak said. Authorities also seized at least four phones from his car and person, and electronic equipment from his home.Sixteen people, including five foreigners, two police officers and the attacker, were taken to hospital. The interior ministry later said they were from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia.Speaking on Sunday, one of two surgeons who treated victims on the street after the attack said his colleague "undoubtedly" saved the life of a gravely injured police officer.The two surgeons, who were eating near the Main Market Square when the gunman opened fire, rushed to the scene to treat both the attacker and the two injured police officers. Professor Michal Pędziwiatr told the BBC: "We saw the shooting attack. And what a surgeon can do in a situation like this?... We decided to help the victims as soon as possible.""We rushed into the area where the shooting was and started our rescue, because there were no ambulances available, there were no professionals around."Pędziwiatr said his colleague, who has been named by local media as Dr Mateusz Wierdak, used his hand to stem the bleeding from the most severely injured policeman, allowing time for an ambulance to arrive.On Sunday it was reported that both injured officers had emerged from comas.Witnesses who were near the Main Market Square have described their panic and confusion as the attack unfolded. Ruby, from London, heard gunfire and "yelled at my friends to run and we all sprinted for our lives".She said they "just kept sprinting" until they found a hotel to shelter inside. Tom Brook, from West Yorkshire, was inside a McDonald's near the square when he heard "multiple gunshots and saw people running for cover"."I then walked into the square and saw paramedics working on someone outside [a shop] and there was a dead body covered in foil blankets 20 metres away," he said.

schema.headline: Krakow shooting suspect has died in hospital, police say

title: Why now's not the time to put your feet up before Christmas
description: Doing these things now will help you save money at ChristmasImage source, Getty/ Tanja IvanovaByCost of living correspondentHow soon is too soon when
body: Doing these things now will help you save money at ChristmasImage source, Getty/ Tanja IvanovaByCost of living correspondentHow soon is too soon when it comes to thinking about Christmas and your finances?The answer, of course, is that it is never too soon. Save early and the cost becomes more manageable.The squeeze is harder for some than others, with charity Barnardo's warning that some parents will skip meals so their kids get a Christmas dinner with the trimmings.But, debt advice charity StepChange is offering tips to everyone, to avoid Christmas spending leading to a financially painful new year.What to think about nowThe best way to avoid a difficult January, it says, is to make a realistic plan before the spending begins. Small decisions now can make a big difference later. Its tips include:Budget for Christmas in full. So, that's not just presents, a budget should include the cost of food and drink, travel, parties, presents, postage, decorations and other festive extrasSpread the cost. Don't just rely on your December paypacket. Also, make a shopping list before Black Friday on 27 November - it is only a discount if you were going to buy it anywayBook your train journey now. Advance tickets, if available, are cheaperSet spending limits. Put a cap on the bill for Christmas socialising, and have a quiet conversation with family and friends about how much to spend on presentsStocktake before the big food shop. Check your cupboards, fridge and freezer before you go shopping and plan meals around food you already have. Make a list of what you need and compare prices.Think twice. Can you afford what you are going to buy? Can you afford the repayments if it's bought on credit? And, do you really need it?"Christmas is a time when we want to enjoy ourselves and make things special for the people we care most about," said Vikki Brownridge, chief executive of StepChange."But it can also put a lot of pressure on household budgets, and it is key to take steps to get ahead of any January financial blues."Where to go for helpIf you are concerned about Christmas leaving you in debt, then it is best to seek advice well before things become unmanageable. The independent MoneyHelper website has a guide to finding free debt advice near you, external.There are also tools to work out if you are receiving all the benefits and grants you are entitled to, and tips on how to draw up a budget.And it is really important to watch out for scams at this time of year. Fraudsters will take any opportunity to catch you out, especially when you are under pressure financially.Get in touchHow have you been affected by the issues raised in this story? Get in touch.

title: 'Electrical items sparked' fire that killed mum and kids on Boxing Day
description: Electrical items caused fatal fire, inquest hearsImage source, FacebookImage caption, Fionnghuala Shearman was killed in an accidental house fire alon
body: Electrical items caused fatal fire, inquest hearsImage source, FacebookImage caption, Fionnghuala Shearman was killed in an accidental house fire along with her children, Eve and Ohner, on Boxing Day last yearByWill GlennonChloe Harcombe and Jasmine Ketibuah-FoleyWest of EnglandA house fire on Boxing Day last year which killed a woman and her two children is believed to have been caused by electrical appliances, an inquest has heard.Fionnghuala Mary Shearman, 38, known as Nu, her seven-year-old daughter Eve and her son Ohner, four, died at their home in Brimscombe, Gloucestershire, in the early hours of 26 December last year.Partner and serving police officer Tom Shearman, escaped and tried to re-enter the house multiple times to save his wife and children, but was unable to due to the severity of the blaze.Leroy Hughes, from Gloucestershire Fire and Rescue Service said items such as soft furnishings and the Christmas tree would likely have fueled the flames.An inquest held at Gloucestershire Coroner's Court on Monday heard the fire likely started in the living room, caused by electrical items connected to the mains power supply.Emergency services were called at 03:12 GMT and crews found the property "well alight", according to Hughes.Shearman told the court he had noticed an "unusual warmth and a smoky atmosphere" in the house when he got up to use the bathroom shortly after 03:00 GMT. He attempted to wake his family when he realised the house was on fire, but was unable to reach them despite "striking and kicking" a window from outside.When his efforts were to no avail, Shearman broke into a neighbouring property to help the occupant leave to "prevent the further loss of life".The inquest heard the neighbour, called June, had spent Christmas morning having coffee and cake with the family before the tragedy unfolded.Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, The fire is believed to have been caused by electrical appliancesThe inquest was told emergency services arrived at the scene to find Mr Shearman outside the property in a "very distressed state" and having sustained "quite significant injuries".The fire destroyed the roof, the ceilings and stairs, as well as causing other significant internal damage to the house.Senior coroner Katy Skerrett paid tribute to Mr Shearman's "valiant" attempts to save his family.The coroner said she accepted the fire had likely started in the living room of the property and added that it was probable the fire had started "from an electric ignition source".The cause of death for all three family members was given as "exposure to the combustion products of fire" and the coroner concluded they were accidental deaths, describing it as an "absolute tragedy with the most horrific consequences possible for this loving young family".Figure caption, Shearman said previously family and friends had "rallied around" to provide him with housing, clothes and food as well as "company and compassion".In a tribute paid to his family on a GoFundMe appeal, he said previously: "My life, the lives of my loved ones, my friends and the whole community changed on Boxing Day."My family had its very core, its very essence, ripped from it in the most violent way."I cannot begin to describe the anguish and trauma of the events of Boxing Day 2025."I will heal."Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: 'Electrical items sparked' fire that killed mum and kids on Boxing Day

title: Republican Thomas Massie will force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth
description: A Republican congressman plans to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, alleging he has vi
body: A Republican congressman plans to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, alleging he has violated the US Constitution."By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorisation, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable," Representative Thomas Massie said.The effort will likely fail, as Republicans remain in power in Congress until January. But Massie says the effort is aimed at pushing President Donald Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.Hegseth has called the impeachment effort a "sham" and defended his record."You see, they attack me. They attack us because we are effective," he said in a video statement last week. "It's not going to work. We will not back down."He called Massie a "disgruntled, defeated congressman" and said he was not concerned about the impeachment effort. In the video, Hegseth defended his leadership of the department and listed ways he has fulfilled Trump's America First agenda.Massie formally introduced his articles of impeachment in a resolution on the House floor on Monday afternoon. The move starts a 48-hour clock for the chamber to take up the measure. Lawmakers could vote on the resolution directly, vote to refer it to committee or to set it aside."I'm doing this because it's the right thing to do," he told reporters after introducing the articles.Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it started nearly nine months ago. He has previously garnered headlines over demanding the Trump administration release the files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.The Kentucky congressman first introduced impeachment articles in September and has now brought them back in the wake of Republicans losing control of both the House and Senate in last week's midterm elections. He has said the effort was aimed at preventing a Democrat spectacle next year when they have control of Congress. He said he hoped to force Trump to name a replacement, who could be quickly confirmed while Republicans have power. "My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what's coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year," Massie also said in a statement. "They will hold hearings and trials."Democratic leadership has signalled openness to such an effort against Hegseth once they take control in January. Asked about the effort on Monday, Hegseth said, "We're not worried about that". He said he planned to hold a news conference on Tuesday to discuss the subject. Impeaching a cabinet secretary is rare. It must be approved by both chambers for the secretary to be removed from office. Trump was impeached by the House twice in his first term in office but was cleared by the Senate after two trials and not removed.  As with the presidential process, the House would first hold a vote on charges against Hegseth and the Senate then would conduct a trial to decide whether to acquit or convict.The House has voted to impeach only two cabinet members in US history, but the Senate did not convict either one.While impeachment has been "an incredibly rare process", it has become far more normalised since the House impeached President Bill Clinton in 1998, said Paul Gowder, a law professor at Northwestern University in Chicago. He said it has become "much more common as the country has become more politically polarised," adding a prediction that several more of Trump's cabinet members may face impeachment over the next two years. Massie told reporters he was not sure if the measure had sufficient backing to pass. It would need a majority to pass the House and even with all Democratic support, it would still likely need some Republican support as the party holds a slim majority. Peter Loge, a professor of public affairs at George Washington University, told the BBC that he believed it was likely to pass due to those slim margins. "There are enough angry Republicans that more than enough Republicans are gonna simply not show up to vote," he said.Currently, there are 218 Republicans and 214 Democrats in the House.While the House requires a simple majority to pass articles of impeachment, the Senate mandates a two-thirds vote to convict, threshold that is difficult to meet in the current congressional term. When Democrats take over in January, they are likely to have at least 54 Senate seats - though two races do not yet have winners due to slim voting margins. A total of 60 votes will be required to convict and remove an official from office.

schema.headline: Republican Thomas Massie will force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth

title: Poundland unable to buy new stock as fears over collapse grow
description: Poundland is unable to buy new stock to fill its shelves after being blocked by its owners from accessing cash in its bank accounts.The discount chain
body: Poundland is unable to buy new stock to fill its shelves after being blocked by its owners from accessing cash in its bank accounts.The discount chain is on the brink of collapse with one insider describing it as "running on fumes". It has until Thursday to secure a rescue deal.About £50m has been frozen by its American owner Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning its 600 shops are running out of stock.Pressure is building on Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland for £1 last June, after the owner rejected a takeover bid that could have saved the thousands of jobs currently at risk. Gordon Brothers has been approached for comment.Poundland has filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which protects it from its creditors until Thursday. Access to funds was limited because of a tension between Gordon Brothers' dual role as both creditor and shareholder, a source said, but added they expected a relaxation of funds in the next two days.Last week, Poundland boss Barry Williams told staff like-for-like sales, which exclude new store openings, were up 11.4% last week, which included Halloween, but said this was £1.5m ahead of budget.He said the business made a profit of £18.1m in the year to September, which was a "strong recovery" from the previous year where the business made losses of £68m. The latest annual accounts have yet to be audited.On Thursday, the 10-day moratorium to protect Poundland from its creditors expires, but if there is a prospect of a solvent deal, the deadline could be extended. If not, Poundland is set to collapse into administration and could be broken up.A source familiar with the sales process said London-based Xyra Group was making "significant progress" in its last minute bid to buy Poundland and could now be the front runner. An extension of Thursday's deadline now seems an increasingly likely scenario. But such a case would be difficult to put forward if Gordon Brothers continues to block funding.One observer remarked "if Gordon Brothers is going in front of that committee, you don't want to be giving the message we're pulling up the drawbridge".Even if a deal is agreed to sell the business as a whole, there is no guarantee a new owner would not reduce the number of stores, but suppliers to Poundland would prefer that outcome to hundreds of sites being sold off to other retailers.There has been interest from the likes of Poundstretcher, Tesco and B&M in picking up stores which could mean continuing employment for many workers.The central issue is whether a piecemeal sale would protect more jobs than a buyer willing to keep Poundland trading as a national chain.

schema.headline: Poundland unable to buy new stock as fears over collapse grow
